title: Striding Garuda (The Royal Solar Bird)

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Samuel Eilenberg Collection, Ex Coll.: Columbia University, Purchase, Mr. and Mrs. Nathan Halpern Gift, 1987

altText: A very small bronze sculpture of a Garuda, a mythical bird, shown in a striding pose. The dark metal surface is cast in a compact shape, about the size of a fist.

context: A small bronze figure of Garuda, a mythical bird of Hindu and Buddhist stories, made in what is now Thailand in the Angkor period, in the third quarter of the 10th century. The Met's title calls it 'The Royal Solar Bird', and the sculpture is only about 13 cm tall.

descriptions.k: This tiny bronze statue shows Garuda. Garuda is a magical bird from old stories. He is striding, like he is taking a big step. The statue is only as big as your hand. What would Garuda do next?
descriptions.g12: Garuda is a magical bird from stories told in Asia long ago. This bronze statue shows him striding forward, as if he is on the move. It is very small, only about as tall as a juice box. The artist cast metal into a strong shape. What do you think Garuda is heading toward?
descriptions.g35: In stories from India and Southeast Asia, Garuda is a giant, powerful bird. This small bronze, made about a thousand years ago in what is now Thailand, shows him mid-stride. Its title calls him 'The Royal Solar Bird,' a clue that he was linked with rulers and the sun. Study the pose. How can a tiny statue still feel strong and important?
descriptions.g68: Garuda, a mythical bird in Hindu and Buddhist traditions, was often linked with power, speed, and royalty. This bronze, made in the Angkor period in the 10th century, shows him striding. At only about 13 cm tall, it is small enough to hold, yet the pose gives it energy. Its title, 'The Royal Solar Bird,' suggests associations with the sun and kings. How might a sculptor give a small object a sense of power?
descriptions.g910: This 10th-century bronze presents Garuda in motion, using a striding pose to suggest purpose and authority. The Met's title, 'The Royal Solar Bird,' points to the creature's association with the sun and with rulers, a link found widely in Southeast Asian art of the Angkor period. Its small scale, about 13 cm, raises questions about use: devotion, display, or ritual. How do pose, scale, and metal combine to create presence, and what can we responsibly infer about function?
descriptions.g1112: Garuda was a prominent emblem in Angkor-period culture, associated with divine power and royal authority, and this small bronze condenses that status into a striding figure. The Met's title stresses solar and royal associations, but the record does not specify the object's original function, so claims about ritual use, mounting, or patronage remain tentative. Consider how scale, casting, and gesture communicate force, and how a mythical hybrid can express ideals of rulership across Hindu and Buddhist contexts.

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Sculpture), medium (Bronze), culture, and tag (Mythical Creatures) checked against the museum record. The Met catalog page has no label text, so descriptions rely on the title and general knowledge of Garuda and stay hedged about detail. Bare-chested or human-like body features could not be ruled out from metadata alone.

teacherNote.context: A small bronze (about 13 cm) of Garuda, a mythical bird of Hindu and Buddhist traditions, from Thailand in the Angkor period, third quarter of the 10th century. The record gives no information about its original use.
directions: Have students sketch the statue's silhouette and describe the movement it suggests.
Compare Garuda with another mythical creature students know, such as a dragon or phoenix, and discuss what each symbolizes.
Discuss how scale affects the way we value and use objects.
